questions.question: When a glass rod is rubbed with a silk cloth the charge acquired by glass rod is
questions.answer:
**(A)** Positive

Rubbing transfers electrons from the glass to the silk. Glass is triboelectrically positive — it loses electrons and is left with a deficit, so it becomes positively charged, while the silk gains those electrons and becomes equally negative. The two charges are always equal and opposite, because charging by friction only *separates* charge; no charge is created.

questions.question: An object has a negative charge of 1 coulomb. The number of excess electrons on it is
questions.answer:
**(D)** $6.25\times10^{18}$

Charge is quantised, $Q=ne$, with $e=1.6\times10^{-19}$ C. For a charge of 1 C,

$$n=\frac{Q}{e}=\frac{1}{1.6\times10^{-19}}=6.25\times10^{18}$$

Since the body is negative it has an *excess* of these electrons. (Option (A) has the wrong sign of exponent and (B) inverts the calculation.)

questions.question: A charge $Q$ is enclosed by a Gaussian spherical surface of radius $R$. If the radius is doubled, then the outward electric flux will
questions.answer:
**(C)** remain unchanged

Gauss's law gives the flux through any closed surface as

$$\phi=\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec S=\frac{Q_{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}$$

The flux depends only on the enclosed charge, not on the size or shape of the surface. Doubling $R$ shrinks $E$ by a factor of 4 at every point, but the area grows by exactly 4, so the product is unchanged.

questions.question: The unit of electric capacitance is
questions.answer:
**(C)** farad

Capacitance is charge per unit potential difference, $C=Q/V$, so its SI unit is coulomb per volt, which is named the farad (F): $1\ \text{F}=1\ \text{C V}^{-1}$. The volt is the unit of potential, the newton of force and the ampere of current.

questions.question: If a uniform wire of resistance 16 $\Omega$ is cut into four equal parts and attached in parallel combination, the equivalent resistance of the combination is
questions.answer:
**(A)** 1 $\Omega$

A uniform wire of resistance $16\ \Omega$ cut into four equal lengths gives four pieces of $16/4=4\ \Omega$ each (resistance is proportional to length). Four equal resistors $R$ in parallel give $R/4$:

$$R_{eq}=\frac{4\ \Omega}{4}=1\ \Omega$$

Note the general result: cutting a wire into $n$ equal parts and joining them in parallel reduces the resistance by $n^2$ ($16/16=1\ \Omega$).

questions.question: Drift velocity $V_d$ varies with the intensity of electric field $E$ as per the relation
questions.answer:
**(D)** $V_d\propto E$

Between collisions the field gives each electron an acceleration $a=eE/m$, and the average time between collisions is the relaxation time $\tau$. Hence

$$v_d=a\tau=\frac{eE}{m}\tau\ \Rightarrow\ v_d\propto E$$

This linear relation is the microscopic origin of Ohm's law, since $I=neAv_d$ and $V=El$ then give $V\propto I$.

questions.question: Two long parallel wires each carrying a current of 1 A in the same direction, are placed 1 m apart. The force of attraction between them is
questions.answer:
**(C)** $2\times10^{-7}$ N/m

The force per unit length between two long parallel wires is

$$\frac{F}{l}=\frac{\mu_0 I_1I_2}{2\pi d}$$

With $I_1=I_2=1$ A and $d=1$ m,

$$\frac{F}{l}=\frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times1\times1}{2\pi\times1}=2\times10^{-7}\ \text{N m}^{-1}$$

Currents in the *same* direction attract — this is the basis of the old definition of the ampere. (Option (A) simply omits the $10^{-7}$.)

questions.question: In a uniform magnetic field $B$ a conductor of length $l$ is placed parallel to the magnetic field. When a current $I$ is passed through the conductor, the force on the conductor will be
questions.answer:
**(D)** zero

The magnetic force on a current element is $\vec F=I\,\vec l\times\vec B$, whose magnitude is $F=IlB\sin\theta$ where $\theta$ is the angle between the conductor and the field. Here the conductor is *parallel* to $\vec B$, so $\theta=0$ and $\sin\theta=0$: the force vanishes. The force is maximum ($IlB$) when the conductor is perpendicular to the field.

questions.question: The magnetic lines of force inside a bar magnet
options: depend on area of cross-section of the bar magnet
are from $N$-pole to $S$-pole of the magnet
are from $S$-pole to $N$-pole of the magnet
questions.answer:
**(D)** are from $S$-pole to $N$-pole of the magnet

Magnetic field lines are closed curves. Outside the magnet they run from the north pole to the south pole; *inside* they must therefore continue from the south pole back to the north pole, so that the loop closes. This is unlike electric field lines, which start on positive and end on negative charge and are not closed.

questions.question: Which of the following materials is most suitable for making a permanent magnet?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Steel

A good permanent magnet needs high **retentivity** (it keeps a large remanent magnetism) together with high **coercivity** (it is hard to demagnetise). Steel — hard iron with carbon — has a wide hysteresis loop and retains its magnetism, whereas soft iron has a narrow loop, high permeability and low coercivity, making it ideal for *electro*magnets where the field must be switched off quickly. Nickel is magnetic but weaker, and copper is not ferromagnetic at all.

questions.question: Wb/m$^2$ is the unit of
questions.answer:
**(A)** magnetic field

Magnetic flux $\Phi$ is measured in weber (Wb), and magnetic flux density is flux per unit area, $B=\Phi/A$, so its unit is Wb/m$^2$ — exactly the tesla. Magnetic flux itself is in Wb, magnetic potential in A (ampere-turns) and magnetic moment in A m$^2$.

questions.question: The self-inductance of a coil is measured by
questions.answer:
**(C)** Induced $emf$

Self-inductance is defined through Faraday's law for the coil itself: $e=-L\,dI/dt$, so $L$ is the back emf produced per unit rate of change of current. Because of this opposing emf, inductance is loosely called the *electrical inertia* of the circuit, but the quantity actually measured is the induced emf (for example by comparing it in a bridge with a known inductance).

questions.question: The unit of inductance is
questions.answer:
**(A)** henry

From $e=-L\,dI/dt$, $L=e/(dI/dt)$, so $1\ \text{H}=1\ \text{V s A}^{-1}$ (one volt per ampere per second). The weber is the unit of magnetic flux, the newton of force and the ohm of resistance: $1\ \text{H}=1\ \text{Wb A}^{-1}$ follows from $\Phi=LI$.

questions.question: The mean value of an alternating current in a half cycle is
questions.answer:
**(C)** $\frac{2I_0}{\pi}$

For $I=I_0\sin\omega t$ the average over a half cycle is

$$I_{av}=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi}I_0\sin\theta\,d\theta=\frac{I_0}{\pi}\big[-\cos\theta\big]_0^{\pi}=\frac{2I_0}{\pi}\approx0.637I_0$$

(Over a *full* cycle the mean is zero.) The value $I_0/\sqrt2$ is the r.m.s. value and $I_0/2$ is the half-period average of the *power* term, not the current.

questions.question: Which of the following has the smallest wavelength?
questions.answer:
**(D)** $\gamma$-rays

Wavelength decreases across the spectrum in the order radio > micro-wave > infrared > visible > ultraviolet > X-ray > $\gamma$-ray. Gamma rays have wavelengths below about $10^{-11}$ m — smaller than an atomic nucleus — so among the four listed they are the shortest. Red light ($\sim700$ nm), ultraviolet ($\sim100$–400 nm) and micro-waves ($\sim$ mm–cm) are all far longer.

questions.question: Which electromagnetic radiation is used for photography in fog?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Infrared ray

Infrared radiation has a wavelength much longer than the size of the water droplets and dust particles of fog, so it is scattered far less than visible light — just as long-wavelength radio waves diffract round obstacles. Infrared photography therefore sees through haze and fog and works in darkness. Ultraviolet and X-rays are strongly absorbed or scattered by the atmosphere, and radio waves are far too long to form a photographic image.

questions.question: The image formed by a simple microscope is
questions.answer:
**(A)** imaginary and erect

A simple microscope is a single convex lens of short focal length used with the object placed *between* the lens and its focus ($u<f$). The rays leave the lens diverging, so a virtual, erect and magnified image is seen at the near point (or at infinity for relaxed viewing). A real image would have to be formed on a screen on the far side and would be inverted.

questions.question: Refraction takes place due to
options: change in the speed of light
no change in the speed of light
change in the colour of light
questions.answer:
**(A)** change in the speed of light

Light travels at $c/n$ in a medium of refractive index $n$. At a boundary between two media of different $n$ the speed must change, and the wavefront must stay continuous across the boundary — the result is the bending called refraction, with Snell's law $n_1\sin i=n_2\sin r$. Colour and polarisation are not required for refraction; even monochromatic, unpolarised light refracts.

questions.question: The concept of secondary wavelets was given by
questions.answer:
**(C)** Huygens

Huygens (1678) proposed that every point on a wavefront acts as a fresh source of secondary wavelets, and the new wavefront is their envelope. Fresnel later supplied the mathematical amplitude/intensity treatment (Huygens–Fresnel principle); Newton held the rival corpuscular theory and Maxwell gave the electromagnetic nature of light.

questions.question: The size of the obstacle for the diffraction of light should be
options: much larger than the wavelength of light
much smaller than the wavelength of light
of the order of wavelength of light
questions.answer:
**(C)** of the order of wavelength of light

Diffraction is the bending of waves round the edges of an obstacle, and it is appreciable only when the obstacle or aperture is comparable in size to the wavelength — then the path differences between secondary wavelets are of the order of one wavelength. When the obstacle is much larger than $\lambda$ the fringe pattern collapses against the geometrical shadow and light travels essentially in straight lines.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Photoelectric effect supports
questions.answer:
**(B)** particle nature of light

The photoelectric effect cannot be explained by the wave theory: the maximum kinetic energy depends on *frequency* alone, not on intensity, and there is a threshold frequency below which no emission occurs however intense the beam; emission is also practically instantaneous. Einstein's photon picture, $h\nu=\phi_0+K_{max}$, explains all of this, so the effect establishes the particle (quantum) nature of light.

questions.question: The force which causes scattering of alpha particles in Rutherford's alpha particle scattering experiment is
questions.answer:
**(B)** Coulomb force

An $\alpha$-particle is heavy, so the gravitational force on it from a nucleus is negligible, and it is non-magnetic. What deflects it is the electrostatic repulsion between its charge $+2e$ and the positive nuclear charge $+Ze$; for a head-on approach,

$$K=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{(2e)(Ze)}{r_0}$$

gives the very small distance of closest approach. The strong nuclear force acts only at ranges smaller than this and does not come into play.

questions.question: The equivalent energy of 10 g of substance is
questions.answer:
**(A)** $9\times10^{14}$ J

By Einstein's mass-energy relation,

$$E=mc^{2}=(10\times10^{-3}\ \text{kg})(3\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1})^{2}=9\times10^{14}\ \text{J}$$

For comparison, this is about the energy released by a 200-kiloton nuclear explosion. (Option (B) uses $c=3\times10^{7}$ and (C) uses $10^{-2}$ kg by mistake.)

questions.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.question: In $n$-type semiconductor what kind of impurity is found?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Valency of five

An $n$-type crystal is doped with a **pentavalent** impurity — phosphorus, arsenic, antimony or bismuth — whose five valence electrons leave one over after bonding with four silicon neighbours. That loosely bound electron is easily freed into the conduction band, so electrons are the majority carrier (hence $n$-type). Trivalent impurities give $p$-type material.

questions.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.question: The width of forbidden band is maximum for
questions.answer:
**(B)** non-conductors

In a conductor the conduction and valence bands overlap, so the forbidden gap is effectively zero. In a semiconductor the gap is small ($\approx1.1$ eV for Si, $0.7$ eV for Ge) and thermal energy can promote electrons across it. In an insulator (non-conductor) the gap is large — about $6$ eV for diamond — so practically no electrons reach the conduction band at ordinary temperatures.

questions.question: What is the dielectric constant of a metal?
questions.answer:
**Its dielectric constant is infinite** ($K\to\infty$).

$K$ measures how strongly a material is polarised by an applied field, and $K=\varepsilon/\varepsilon_0$. In a metal the free electrons move until they cancel the internal field completely: the field inside a conductor in equilibrium is zero, so $E=E_0/K\to0$ requires $K\to\infty$. Equivalently, a metal behaves as a medium of zero permittivity for the *net* field, which is why static charge resides entirely on its surface.

questions.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.question: What is the S.I. unit of mobility ($\mu$)?
questions.answer:
**m$^2$ V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$** (metre squared per volt per second).

Mobility is drift velocity per unit electric field, $\mu=v_d/E$, so its unit is $(\text{m s}^{-1})/(\text{V m}^{-1})=\text{m}^{2}\text{V}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$. For electrons in silicon it is about $0.135\ \text{m}^2\text{V}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$.

questions.question: Which law determines the direction of an induced current?
questions.answer:
**Lenz's law.**

It states that the induced current is set up in such a direction that it opposes the very change which produces it, $e=-d\Phi/dt$ — the minus sign being the statement of the law. For example, when a magnet is pushed north-pole-first towards a coil, the face of the coil turned towards the magnet becomes a north pole, so the induced current opposes the approach. Lenz's law is a consequence of the conservation of energy.

questions.question: Mention any one property of electromagnetic waves.
questions.answer:
**They are transverse waves** — the oscillating electric field $\vec E$ and magnetic field $\vec B$ are both perpendicular to the direction of propagation and to each other, so they can be polarised.

*(Any one of the standard properties is acceptable, e.g. they travel in vacuum with the same speed $c=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}=3\times10^{8}$ m/s, need no material medium, carry momentum $p=U/c$, or show the phenomena of reflection, refraction, interference and diffraction.)*

questions.question: When light passes from a denser medium to a rarer medium, and the angle of incidence equals the critical angle, what is the angle of refraction?
questions.answer:
**It is $90^{\circ}$** — the refracted ray grazes along the surface separating the two media.

By Snell's law $n_1\sin C=n_2\sin 90^{\circ}=n_2$, so $\sin C=n_2/n_1=1/{}^{1}\!n_2$. At the critical angle the refracted ray just travels along the boundary; for any angle of incidence greater than $C$ refraction cannot occur at all and the light is totally internally reflected.

questions.question: What do you understand by the term 'diffraction of light'?
questions.answer:
**Diffraction of light is its bending round the edges of an obstacle or the spreading out of light after passing through a narrow aperture**, so that the intensity is not simply cut off at the geometrical shadow but forms a pattern of alternate bright and dark fringes.

It occurs whenever the size of the obstacle or slit is comparable with the wavelength of light, and it is a direct consequence of Huygens' principle: the secondary wavelets from different parts of the open aperture superpose with different path differences.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Define work function of metal.
questions.answer:
**The work function of a metal is the minimum energy required to just eject an electron from its surface** (i.e. to bring an electron from the Fermi level to rest just outside the metal).

It is denoted $\phi_0$ (or $W$) and measured in electron-volts; for caesium it is about 2.14 eV and for platinum about 5.65 eV. In Einstein's photoelectric equation, $h
u=\phi_0+K_{max}$, so emission occurs only if $h
u\ge\phi_0$, which sets the threshold frequency $
u_0=\phi_0/h$.

questions.question: What do you mean by mass defect of a nucleus?
questions.answer:
**The mass defect is the difference between the sum of the masses of the free protons and neutrons that make up a nucleus and the actual mass of the nucleus:**

$$\Delta m=[Zm_p+(A-Z)m_n]-M_{\text{nucleus}}$$

It is always positive, and the corresponding energy $\Delta m\,c^{2}$ is the binding energy that holds the nucleons together — the energy which must be supplied to split the nucleus into free nucleons. For helium, $\Delta m\approx0.0304$ u giving $E_b\approx28.3$ MeV.

questions.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.question: What are majority charge carriers in a $n$-type semiconductor?
questions.answer:
**Electrons.**

Doping with a pentavalent impurity such as phosphorus donates one loosely bound electron per impurity atom into the conduction band, so the electron concentration greatly exceeds the hole concentration ($n_e\gg n_h$). Electrons are therefore the majority carriers in $n$-type material and holes the minority carriers, the product $n_en_h=n_i^{2}$ still holding.

questions.question: Derive an expression for the electric field at a point on equatorial (broad side on) position of an electric dipole.
questions.answer:
**Equatorial point.** Let the dipole be $+q$ at $A$ and $-q$ at $B$, separated by $2a$, and let $P$ be a point on the perpendicular bisector at distance $r$ from the centre $O$, with $r\gg a$.

![Dipole equatorial point](dip)

The field at $P$ due to $+q$ is $E_{+}=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^{2}+a^{2}}$ along $AP$ (directed away from $+q$), and that due to $-q$ is $E_{-}=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^{2}+a^{2}}$ along $PB$ (directed towards $-q$). The two are equal in magnitude, so resolving them: the components along $\vec{AB}$ oppose and cancel, while the components along $OP$ add up. If $\angle OAP=\theta$,

$$E=E_{+}\cos\theta+E_{-}\cos\theta=2E_{+}\cos\theta$$

where $\cos\theta=\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{r^{2}+a^{2}}}$. Hence

$$E=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{2qa}{\left(r^{2}+a^{2}\right)^{3/2}}$$

Using $p=2qa$ and taking $r\gg a$,

$$\boxed{\;E_{eq}=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{p}{\left(r^{2}+a^{2}\right)^{3/2}}\approx\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{p}{r^{3}}\;}$$

The resultant field is **antiparallel to the dipole moment** (it points from the $+q$ side towards the $-q$ side). Comparing with the axial field $E_{ax}=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{2p}{r^{3}}$, the equatorial field is half the axial field at the same distance, and both fall off as $1/r^{3}$ rather than $1/r^{2}$.

questions.topic: Potential due to a Point Charge
questions.question: Derive an expression for electric potential at a point due to a point charge.
questions.answer:
**Electric potential** at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a test charge from infinity to that point without acceleration.

![Point charge potential](pot)

Consider a point charge $+Q$ at the origin and a point $P$ at distance $r$. At an intermediate point a distance $x$ from $Q$, the field is

$$E=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{x^{2}}$$

The work done in moving a unit charge from $x$ to $x+dx$ is $-E\,dx$ (negative, since the displacement is against the field). So the work bringing a unit charge from infinity to $P$:

$$V=-\int_{\infty}^{r}E\,dx=-\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_{\infty}^{r}\frac{dx}{x^{2}}=-\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[-\frac1x\right]_{\infty}^{r}$$

$$\boxed{\;V=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{r}\;}$$

For a negative charge the potential is negative, i.e. $V=-\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{|Q|}{r}$ — work must be done *against* the attractive force to bring the test charge in from infinity.

Since potential is a scalar, the potential of a system of charges is the algebraic sum $V=\sum\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q_i}{r_i}$, and for a continuous distribution $V=\int\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{dq}{r}$.

questions.question: How can a galvanometer be converted into a ammeter? Calculate the effective resistance of the ammeter.
questions.answer:
**Conversion to an ammeter.** A galvanometer alone cannot measure large currents — its coil would burn out — and it must be connected in *series* with the circuit, so it needs a very low resistance. It is therefore converted into an ammeter by connecting a **low resistance (shunt) $S$ in parallel** with it.

The shunt carries most of the current, and only a small fraction passes through the galvanometer. If $G$ is the galvanometer resistance, $I_g$ the current for full-scale deflection and $I$ the maximum current to be measured, the p.d. across the two parallel paths is the same:

$$I_gG=(I-I_g)S\ \Rightarrow\ S=\frac{I_gG}{I-I_g}$$

**Effective resistance.** The ammeter resistance is the parallel combination of $G$ and $S$:

$$R_A=\frac{GS}{G+S}$$

Substituting $S$ and simplifying,

$$R_A=\frac{I_g}{I}G$$

Since $I_g\ll I$, $R_A$ is much smaller than $G$ — exactly what an ammeter needs, because an ammeter is inserted in series and must not change the current it measures. Specifically, to increase the range $n=I/I_g$ times, $S=\dfrac{G}{n-1}$ and $R_A=G/n$.

questions.question: Derive an expression for the coefficient of mutual induction of two long coaxial solenoids.
questions.answer:
Take two long coaxial solenoids: the inner one of radius $r_1$, length $l$ and $N_1$ turns, and the outer of radius $r_2$, length $l$ and $N_2$ turns wound over it ($l\gg r_2$, so end effects are negligible).

Let a current $I_2$ flow in the outer solenoid. The field it produces inside is uniform and axial:

$$B_2=\mu_0 n_2 I_2,\qquad n_2=\frac{N_2}{l}$$

This field passes through the inner solenoid, linking each of its $N_1$ turns over the area $A=\pi r_1^{2}$ (only the area of the inner solenoid carries flux). Hence the flux linkage is

$$N_1\Phi_1=N_1B_2A=N_1\left(\mu_0\frac{N_2}{l}I_2\right)\pi r_1^{2}$$

By definition $N_1\Phi_1=M_{12}I_2$, so

$$\boxed{\;M=\mu_0\frac{N_1N_2}{l}\pi r_1^{2}=\frac{\mu_0N_1N_2\pi r_1^{2}}{l}\;}$$

Writing it as $M=\mu_0n_1n_2\,Al$, this is the flux-linked-per-unit-current of the pair; since the flux due to the inner solenoid passes wholly through the outer one, the same value results whether the current is set up in the inner or the outer coil — $M_{12}=M_{21}$, as reciprocity requires.

questions.question: Derive an expression for the effective (equivalent) focal length of two thin lenses in contact.
questions.answer:
Two thin lenses of focal lengths $f_1$ and $f_2$ are placed in contact, so that they have a common principal axis and the distance between them is negligible. Let an object $O$ be at distance $u$ from the first lens.

*First lens:* if it alone formed the image, with $v_1$ the image distance,

$$\frac{1}{v_1}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{f_1}\tag{i}$$

*Second lens:* this image $v_1$ acts as the object for the second lens. Because the lenses are in contact, the object distance for the second lens is $v_1$ (it is a virtual object if the first image falls on the far side). If the final image is at $v$,

$$\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{v_1}=\frac{1}{f_2}\tag{ii}$$

Adding (i) and (ii), the $1/v_1$ terms cancel:

$$\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{f_1}+\frac{1}{f_2}$$

But for the combination, which behaves as a single lens of focal length $F$,

$$\frac{1}{v}-\frac{1}{u}=\frac{1}{F}$$

Therefore

$$\boxed{\;\frac{1}{F}=\frac{1}{f_1}+\frac{1}{f_2}\;}$$

In terms of power, $P=P_1+P_2$ — powers add for thin lenses in contact. For $n$ lenses, $\frac1F=\sum\frac{1}{f_i}$. If $f_1=f_2=f$ then $F=f/2$; if one is a convex and the other a concave lens of the same focal length, $F=\infty$ and the combination behaves as a plane glass plate.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Write and explain Einstein's equation of the photoelectric effect.
questions.answer:
**Einstein's photoelectric equation**

$$h\nu=\phi_0+\frac12mv_{max}^{2}\qquad\text{or}\qquad h\nu=h\nu_0+K_{max}$$

**Meaning of the terms.** Light of frequency $\nu$ arrives as photons, each of energy $h\nu$ (one quantum). A single photon is absorbed by a single electron. Of this energy, a fixed minimum amount $\phi_0=h\nu_0$ — the work function of the metal, with $\nu_0$ the threshold frequency — is spent in just freeing the electron from the surface. Whatever is left appears as the maximum kinetic energy $\frac12mv_{max}^{2}$ of the emitted electron.

**Explanations this gives**

- **Threshold frequency:** if $h\nu<\phi_0$ no electron can escape at all, no matter how intense the light — intensity only fixes the *number* of photons.
- **Kinetic energy depends on frequency:** $K_{max}=h\nu-\phi_0$ is linear in $\nu$ with slope $h$, independent of intensity; hence the stopping potential $V_0$ satisfies $eV_0=h\nu-\phi_0$.
- **Instantaneous emission:** a single photon delivers its whole energy at once, so there is no time lag, unlike the wave picture which would need time to accumulate energy.
- **Intensity and current:** doubling intensity doubles the number of photons, hence doubles the saturation photocurrent, without changing $K_{max}$.

Einstein's equation thus established the particle (photon) nature of light and won the explanation that classical wave theory could not give.

questions.question: Mention Rutherford's nuclear atomic model. What are its drawbacks?
questions.answer:
**Rutherford's nuclear model (1911).** From the scattering of $\alpha$-particles by thin metal foils he concluded:

1. Nearly the whole mass and all the positive charge of an atom are concentrated in a very small central region — the **nucleus**, of radius about $10^{-15}$ m, some $10^{5}$ times smaller than the atom ($\sim10^{-10}$ m).
2. The electrons revolve round the nucleus in the empty space around it, the electrostatic attraction supplying the centripetal force — much as planets orbit the Sun.
3. The atom as a whole is electrically neutral, and most of it is empty space, which is why most $\alpha$-particles pass straight through undeflected.

**Drawbacks**

- **Stability of the atom:** an electron revolving in a circle is accelerating, so by classical electrodynamics it must continuously radiate energy. Its orbit would spiral inwards and it would fall into the nucleus in about $10^{-8}$ s — atoms would not be stable, contrary to observation.
- **Origin of line spectra:** as the radius shrinks continuously, the frequency of the emitted radiation should change continuously, giving a continuous spectrum. In fact atoms emit sharp, discrete spectral lines (as in the hydrogen series).
- **No explanation of quantisation:** it says nothing about why electrons occupy only certain orbits, nor can it account for the arrangement of electrons in heavier atoms.

questions.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.question: Write distinguishing features between conductors, semiconductors and insulators based on energy band diagrams.
questions.answer:
**Energy-band picture.** In a solid the allowed electron energies fall into bands: the valence band (filled), the forbidden gap $E_g$, and the conduction band (empty at 0 K). Conductivity depends on how easily electrons cross the gap.

| Feature | Conductors | Semiconductors | Insulators |
|---|---|---|---|
| Forbidden gap $E_g$ | Zero — bands overlap | Small, $\approx1$ eV (Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.7 eV) | Large, $\approx5$–6 eV (diamond $\sim6$ eV) |
| Valence band | Partly filled | Almost full at 0 K | Completely full |
| Conduction band | Partly filled (overlaps) | Empty at 0 K | Empty |
| Carriers at room temp. | Already plentiful | Few, produced thermally ($n\propto e^{-E_g/2k_BT}$) | Practically none |
| Fermi level | Inside the conduction band | Mid-way in the gap | Close to the valence band |
| Resistivity | $\sim10^{-8}\ \Omega$ m | $\sim10^{-5}$–$10^{3}\ \Omega$ m | $>10^{8}\ \Omega$ m |
| Effect of heating | Resistance **increases** (carrier number fixed, lattice scattering grows) | Resistance **decreases** (carriers multiply) | No practical conduction at ordinary $T$ |
| Doping | — | Conductivity can be raised enormously by trivalent/pentavalent impurities | — |

Thus the same band structure explains all three classes: a metal conducts because a band is only partly full, a semiconductor because the gap is small enough for thermal energy to bridge it, and an insulator because the gap is far too wide.

questions.question: State Gauss's law in electrostatics. Using this law derive an expression for the electric field due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet.
questions.answer:
**Statement of Gauss's law.** The total electric flux through any closed surface is equal to $1/\varepsilon_0$ times the net charge enclosed by it:

$$\oint_S\vec E\cdot d\vec S=\frac{Q_{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}$$

It is a consequence of Coulomb's inverse-square law and, because it involves only the enclosed charge, it makes highly symmetric problems easy.

**Field of an infinite plane sheet** of uniform surface charge density $\sigma$.

![Field of a charged sheet](plane)

By symmetry the field must be perpendicular to the sheet and of equal magnitude on both sides. Choose a Gaussian surface in the form of a cylinder (pill-box) with its flat faces of area $A$ parallel to the sheet — one on each side — and its axis perpendicular to it.

- The curved surface is parallel to $\vec E$, so there is no flux through it.
- Through each flat face the flux is $EA$, both outward.

So the total outward flux is

$$\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec S=EA+EA=2EA$$

The charge enclosed is $Q_{enc}=\sigma A$ (only the part of the sheet inside the cylinder). Gauss's law gives

$$2EA=\frac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}\ \Rightarrow\ E=\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$$

$$\boxed{\;\vec E=\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat n\;}$$

**Remarks.** The field is independent of the distance from the sheet — it is uniform on either side and points away from the sheet for positive $\sigma$, towards it for negative $\sigma$. At the surface the field changes discontinuously from $\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$ to $0$ (inside a conductor) in going across it. For two parallel sheets of opposite charge ($\pm\sigma$, a parallel-plate capacitor) the fields add between them and cancel outside, giving $E=\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ between the plates.

questions.question: Mention Kirchhoff's rules for electrical networks and apply them to find an expression for the balance condition for Wheatstone bridge.
questions.answer:
**Kirchhoff's rules**

1. **Junction (current) rule.** The algebraic sum of the currents meeting at any junction is zero: $\sum I=0$. It is simply the conservation of charge — charge cannot accumulate at a junction in the steady state.
2. **Loop (voltage) rule.** Around any closed mesh, the algebraic sum of the products of current and resistance equals the algebraic sum of the emfs: $\sum IR=\sum E$. This is the conservation of energy, since the work done in taking a charge round a closed loop must vanish.

**Wheatstone bridge.** Four resistances $P,Q,R,S$ form a quadrilateral $ABCD$ with the battery across $A$ and $C$ and a galvanometer $G$ between $B$ and $D$; the bridge is balanced when no current flows through the galvanometer.

![Wheatstone bridge](wheat)

Let the current $I$ divide at $A$ into $I_1$ (along $AB$) and $I_2$ (along $AD$). At balance the galvanometer current is zero, so

- the same $I_1$ flows through $B$ to $C$ (through $Q$),
- the same $I_2$ flows through $D$ to $C$ (through $S$),
- $B$ and $D$ are at the same potential, so $V_B-V_D=0$.

**Applying the loop rule.**

Loop $ABDA$: no current through $G$, so $I_1P-I_2R=0$, giving

$$I_1P=I_2R\tag{i}$$

Loop $BCDB$: $I_1Q-I_2S=0$, giving

$$I_1Q=I_2S\tag{ii}$$

Dividing (i) by (ii):

$$\frac{P}{Q}=\frac{R}{S}\qquad\text{or}\qquad \boxed{\;PS=QR\\;}$$

**Condition of balance:** $\dfrac{P}{Q}=\dfrac{R}{S}$. Equivalently, if three resistances are known the fourth is $S=R\,Q/P$ — the principle of the metre bridge, which measures an unknown resistance this way. Interchanging the battery and the galvanometer leaves the balance condition unchanged, and the bridge is most sensitive when all four resistances are of the same order.

questions.question: What is Biot-Savart law? Derive an expression for the magnetic field at a point on the axis of a current carrying circular loop.
questions.answer:
**Biot–Savart law.** The magnetic field $d\vec B$ produced at a point $P$ by a small current element $I\,d\vec l$ is proportional to the current, to the length of the element and to $\sin\theta$ ($\theta$ the angle between the element and the line joining it to $P$), and inversely proportional to the square of the distance:

$$d\vec B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\frac{I\,d\vec l\times\hat r}{r^{2}},\qquad |dB|=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^{2}}$$

The direction is given by $d\vec l\times\hat r$ (right-hand rule). In magnitude form this is the magnetic analogue of Coulomb's law.

**Field on the axis of a circular loop** of radius $a$ carrying current $I$, at a point $P$ a distance $x$ from the centre along the axis.

Consider a current element $I\,dl$ on the loop. Its distance from $P$ is $r=\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}$, and the line joining it to $P$ makes an angle $\theta=90^{\circ}$ with $d\vec l$ (the element is tangent to the circle, the radius to $P$ is perpendicular to it in the plane containing the axis). Hence

$$dB=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,dl}{a^{2}+x^{2}}$$

Resolve $d\vec B$ into a component along the axis, $dB\cos\alpha$, and one perpendicular to the axis, $dB\sin\alpha$, where $\alpha$ is the angle between $d\vec B$ and the axis, with $\cos\alpha=\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}}$.

The perpendicular components from diametrically opposite elements are equal and opposite, so they cancel in pairs over the whole loop. Only the axial components survive:

$$B=\oint dB\cos\alpha=\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi(a^{2}+x^{2})}\cdot\frac{a}{\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}}\oint dl$$

With $\oint dl=2\pi a$,

$$B=\frac{\mu_0 I\,a\,(2\pi a)}{4\pi\left(a^{2}+x^{2}\right)^{3/2}}=\frac{\mu_0Ia^{2}}{2\left(a^{2}+x^{2}\right)^{3/2}}$$

$$\boxed{\;B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2\pi Ia^{2}}{\left(a^{2}+x^{2}\right)^{3/2}}=\frac{\mu_0}{2}\frac{Ia^{2}}{\left(a^{2}+x^{2}\right)^{3/2}}\;}$$

**Special cases.** At the centre ($x=0$), $B=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2a}$; for $x\gg a$, $B\approx\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2(\pi a^{2}I)}{x^{3}}=\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{x^{3}}$, the same $1/x^{3}$ law as the axial field of a magnetic dipole of moment $m=\pi a^{2}I$. If the loop has $N$ turns the field is $N$ times larger.

questions.question:
(a) Derive an expression for average or mean value of alternating current for half cycle.
(b) Derive an expression for root mean square value of alternating current for full cycle.
questions.answer:
Let the alternating current be $I=I_0\sin\omega t$, with $\omega=2\pi/T$.

**(a) Mean value over a half cycle**

The average of $I$ over the half cycle $t=0$ to $t=T/2$ is

$$I_{av}=\frac{1}{T/2}\int_0^{T/2}I_0\sin\omega t\,dt$$

Put $\omega t=\theta$, $d\theta=\omega\,dt$; as $t$ runs $0\to T/2$, $\theta$ runs $0\to\pi$:

$$I_{av}=\frac{I_0}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi}\sin\theta\,d\theta=\frac{I_0}{\pi}\big[-\cos\theta\big]_0^{\pi}=\frac{I_0}{\pi}\left[1-(-1)\right]$$

$$\boxed{\;I_{av}=\frac{2I_0}{\pi}=0.637\,I_0\;}$$

(Over a **full** cycle the integral of $\sin\theta$ from $0$ to $2\pi$ is zero, so the mean of an a.c. over a complete cycle is zero; that is why the half-cycle mean and the r.m.s. value are used.)

**(b) Root mean square value over a full cycle**

The r.m.s. value is the square root of the mean of $I^{2}$ over one complete cycle:

$$I_{rms}^{2}=\frac{1}{T}\int_0^{T}I_0^{2}\sin^{2}\omega t\,dt$$

Put $\omega t=\theta$, so $dt=d\theta/\omega$ and $\theta$ runs $0\to2\pi$:

$$I_{rms}^{2}=\frac{I_0^{2}}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^{2}\theta\,d\theta=\frac{I_0^{2}}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{1-\cos2\theta}{2}\,d\theta$$

$$=\frac{I_0^{2}}{2\pi}\left[\frac{\theta}{2}-\frac{\sin2\theta}{4}\right]_0^{2\pi}=\frac{I_0^{2}}{2\pi}\cdot\pi=\frac{I_0^{2}}{2}$$

$$\boxed{\;I_{rms}=\frac{I_0}{\sqrt2}=0.707\,I_0\;}$$

Since $I^{2}=I_0^{2}\sin^{2}\omega t$ has period $T/2$, the same mean is obtained over a half cycle as over a full one.

**Physical meaning.** The r.m.s. value is that steady current which would produce the same average heating in a resistor: $I_{rms}^{2}R=\overline{I^{2}R}$. This is why a.c. instruments and the 220 V mains rating are quoted as r.m.s. values, and why the peak of the 220 V supply is $220\sqrt2\approx311$ V.

questions.question: Draw ray diagram of a compound microscope. Deduce an expression for its magnifying power when image is formed at near point.
questions.answer:
**Ray diagram.** A compound microscope has two convex lenses: the **objective** (short focal length $f_o$, small aperture) facing the object and the **eyepiece** (focal length $f_e$) near the eye, separated by a tube length $L$.

- The object $AB$ is placed just beyond the objective's focus ($f_o<u_o<2f_o$), so the objective forms a **real, inverted, magnified** image $A'B'$ inside the focal length of the eyepiece.
- The eyepiece then acts as a simple microscope on $A'B'$, forming the final **virtual, inverted (w.r.t. object), magnified** image $A''B''$ at the near point $D=25$ cm.

**Magnifying power** is the angle subtended by the final image at the eye divided by the angle subtended by the object at the unaided eye, when the image is at the near point $D$:

$$M=\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\approx\frac{\tan\beta}{\tan\alpha}$$

For the *eyepiece* alone, the image $A'B'$ at distance $u_e$ from it produces the final image at $D$, so its angular magnification (simple-microscope formula, image at near point) is

$$m_e=1+\frac{D}{f_e}$$

For the *objective*, the linear magnification is $m_o=\dfrac{v_o}{u_o}$. Since $A'B'$ lies just inside the focal plane of the eyepiece, $v_o\approx L$ (objective image distance, nearly the tube length), and using $\dfrac1{f_o}=\dfrac1{v_o}-\dfrac1{u_o}$ one gets $m_o=\dfrac{L}{f_o}$ (with the object just outside $f_o$).

Since the two magnifications multiply,

$$\boxed{\;M=m_o\,m_e=-\frac{v_o}{u_o}\left(1+\frac{D}{f_e}\right)\approx-\frac{L}{f_o}\left(1+\frac{D}{f_e}\right)\;}$$

The minus sign shows the final image is inverted. If instead the final image is formed at infinity (relaxed eye), $m_e=\dfrac{D}{f_e}$ and $M\approx-\dfrac{L\,D}{f_o f_e}$.

**Hence:** for large magnification both focal lengths must be small, which is why microscope lenses are of short focal length; the objective gives the resolving power and the eyepiece the angular magnification.

questions.question: State Huygens' principle. Establish the laws of refraction of light using Huygens' principle.
questions.answer:
**Huygens' principle**

1. Every point on a given wavefront acts as a fresh source of secondary wavelets, which spread out in all directions with the speed of light in that medium.
2. The forward envelope (common tangent surface) of these secondary wavelets at any later instant gives the new position of the wavefront; the backward envelope is ineffective.

**Laws of refraction**

Let a plane wavefront $AB$ strike a plane surface $XY$ separating medium 1 (speed $v_1$, refractive index $n_1$) from medium 2 (speed $v_2$, $n_2$), at angle of incidence $i$.

- Point $A$ reaches the surface first and, in time $t$, sends a secondary wavelet of radius $v_1t$ in medium 1 — but in medium 2 the disturbance from $A$ travels with speed $v_2$.
- Meanwhile $B$ travels to $C$ on the surface, a distance $BC=v_1t$.
- Taking $t$ as the time for the disturbance to go from $B$ to $C$, the distance $BC=v_1t$. During this same time the wavelet from $A$ has grown in medium 2 to a radius $AD=v_2t$.

In the right-angled triangles $ABC$ and $ADC$ (both share the hypotenuse $AC$):

$$\sin i=\frac{BC}{AC}=\frac{v_1t}{AC},\qquad \sin r=\frac{AD}{AC}=\frac{v_2t}{AC}$$

Dividing,

$$\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\frac{v_1}{v_2}$$

Since $n_1=c/v_1$ and $n_2=c/v_2$, this is $\dfrac{v_1}{v_2}=\dfrac{n_2}{n_1}$, so

$$\boxed{\;n_1\sin i=n_2\sin r\;}$$

which is **Snell's law**: the ratio $\sin i/\sin r$ is a constant for the pair of media.

**Second law.** The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal all lie in the same plane — because the secondary wavelets are spherical, the construction is symmetric about the plane containing $AB$, the normal and the surface; the refracted wavefront $CD$ and hence the refracted ray lie in that same plane.

Moreover, since $v_1>v_2$ when medium 1 is the rarer medium, $\sin i>\sin r$, i.e. $i>r$ — light bends towards the normal on entering a denser medium, which is exactly what is observed.
